questions.cardText:
[History] Where does the Silk Road start and end?
A. Beijing to Athens
B. Xi’an to Rome
C. Suzhou to Istanbul
Answer: B.
questions.en: In which present-day Chinese city, the ancient capital Chang'an, did the Silk Road's northern route begin?
questions.de: In welcher heutigen chinesischen Stadt, der alten Hauptstadt Chang'an, begann die nördliche Route der Seidenstraße?

timeline.labelEn: The Silk Road, a network of trade routes between East Asia and the West, active c. 130 BCE to the mid-15th century
timeline.labelDe: Die Seidenstraße, ein Netz von Handelswegen zwischen Ostasien und dem Westen, aktiv von etwa 130 v. Chr. bis Mitte des 15. Jahrhunderts

questions.notes: The card's 'Xi'an to Rome' is a simplification: the Silk Road was a network of routes, not one road with two endpoints. Wikipedia: 'The northern route started at Chang'an (now called Xi'an)'. Asked about the eastern start only.

questions.cardText:
[Zoology] Why is the cookiecutter shark named the cookiecutter shark?
A. It has a round, flat body like it is cut out from a cookiecutter
B. Its body has a pattern that looks like it is cut out from a cookiecutter
C. It leaves wounds on its prey in the shape of a cookie cutter
Answer: C. The cookie-cutter shark uses its sharp, serrated teeth to scoop out plugs of flesh from its prey and has been observed attempting to do the same to submarines and underwater cables.
questions.en: Which small shark is named after the round plugs of flesh it gouges out of its prey, and has also bitten submarines and undersea cables?
questions.de: Welcher kleine Hai ist nach den runden Fleischstücken benannt, die er aus seiner Beute herausbeißt, und hat auch schon U-Boote und Unterseekabel angebissen?

timeline.labelEn: Quoy and Gaimard publish the first description of the cookiecutter shark, as Scymnus brasiliensis
timeline.labelDe: Quoy und Gaimard veröffentlichen die Erstbeschreibung des Zigarrenhais als Scymnus brasiliensis

questions.notes: Asked the other way round. German name: Zigarrenhai (Isistius brasiliensis). Described from the Uranie voyage of 1817–1820, published 1824.
